title: U.S. House · California's 21st Congressional District
area: Fresno, Madera, and Merced counties in the central San Joaquin Valley.

context.text: California redrew its congressional district lines for the 2026 elections under Proposition 50, a mid-decade redistricting measure voters approved in a November 2025 special election.
In the June 2, 2026 top-two primary, Jim Costa won 42.2% of the vote (43,461 votes) and Kyle Kirkland won 26.3% (27,076 votes), advancing them both to the November general election.

candidates.name: Jim Costa
candidates.currentRole: U.S. Representative (since 2005, under various district numbers)

summary.text: Jim Costa is the incumbent Democratic U.S. Representative for California's 21st District, a Fresno-area farmer and former state legislator who has served in the House since 2005. He previously spent 24 years in the California Legislature and is the ranking member of a House Agriculture subcommittee.

background.text: Born April 13, 1952, in Fresno, California, to parents whose families came from the Azores; Wikipedia reports that he grew up working on the family farm and graduated from San Joaquin Memorial High School in 1970.
Earned a B.A. in political science from California State University, Fresno, in 1974.
Worked as a farmer, and early in his career as an aide to Rep. John Krebs and chief of staff to then-Assemblyman Rick Lehman.

Elected to the California State Assembly in 1978 at age 26 and served there until 1994, then in the California State Senate from 1994 to 2002. He sponsored the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act (1995) and served as president of the National Conference of State Legislatures in 2000-2001.

Won an open congressional seat in 2004 after Rep. Cal Dooley retired, defeating Republican state Sen. Roy Ashburn, 53 percent to 47 percent, and took office in January 2005. He has represented the 20th District (2005-2013), the 16th (2013-2023) and the 21st (2023-present).
Serves on the House Agriculture Committee, where he is ranking member of the Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Subcommittee, and on the Foreign Affairs Committee's Europe Subcommittee.

Is a member of the Blue Dog Coalition, New Democrat Coalition, Congressional Hispanic Caucus and Problem Solvers Caucus, and co-founded and co-chairs the Congressional Crime Survivors and Justice Caucus.

priorities.text: Lists expanding healthcare access and affordability in the San Joaquin Valley as a priority, including defending the Affordable Care Act and Medicare and Medicaid funding.
Lists immigration reform rooted in the Valley's economic reality as a priority, including legal status for Dreamers and farmworkers alongside effective border security.
Lists reducing emissions, expanding clean energy, and preventing wildfires as environmental priorities for the San Joaquin Valley.

positions.summary: Helped pass the Affordable Care Act, has defended it from repeal, and voted against 2025 reconciliation legislation that would have cut Medicaid and Medicare funding.
positions.quote: Costa also worked with President Obama and House Democrats to pass the Affordable Care Act (ACA), expanding coverage to over 35 million Americans, protecting 130 million people with pre-existing conditions, and lowering healthcare costs for working families.

positions.summary: Supports legal status for Dreamers and farmworkers while also backing hiring more Border Patrol agents and investing in border-detection technology.
positions.quote: As a member of the House Democrats' Border Security Task Force, Costa supports smart, effective border security, not fear-based politics. He has pushed and voted to hire more border patrol agents, invest in detection technology, and crack down on fentanyl trafficking.

positions.summary: Championed the Inflation Reduction Act, describing it as the largest climate investment in U.S. history, and has funded solar and other renewable-energy projects in his district.
positions.quote: Costa championed the Inflation Reduction Act, the largest climate investment in U.S. history, delivering over $15 million for a first-of-its-kind project to install solar panels over the Delta-Mendota Canal, boosting clean energy while conserving water for Valley farmers and communities.

positions.summary: Voted for the Inflation Reduction Act's 15% corporate minimum tax and 1% excise tax on stock buybacks.
positions.quote: In 2022, he voted to enact the Inflation Reduction Act, which raises $300 billion over the next decade to cut the deficit by requiring large corporations to pay a 15 percent minimum tax on profits and imposing a 1 percent excise tax on stock buybacks.

record.text: Serves on the House Committee on Agriculture (Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Subcommittee) and the House Committee on Foreign Affairs in the 119th Congress.
Co-sponsored the American Dream and Promise Act, which would provide permanent legal status for immigrants brought to the U.S. as children.
Co-authored the Farm Workforce Modernization Act, providing legal status for undocumented farmworkers and modernizing the H-2A visa program.
Introduced the Expanding Medical Education Act to fund medical schools in rural and underserved areas, including plans for full medical schools at UCSF Fresno and UC Merced.

candidates.name: Kyle Kirkland
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the June 2 top-two primary with 26.3% of the vote

summary.text: Kyle Kirkland is a Republican Fresno businessman who owns Club One Casino and is a former chairman of Steinway Musical Instruments. He ran unsuccessfully in the 2024 primaries in the neighboring 20th District, and is challenging Rep. Jim Costa in 2026 on a platform centered on the cost of living.

background.text: According to his 2024 Ballotpedia survey, he was born in Virginia to a teacher and a banker, grew up in Maine, and has lived in California for almost 40 years, the last 15 in the Central Valley.
Earned an A.B. magna cum laude from Harvard College in 1984 and an M.B.A. from the Stanford University Graduate School of Business in 1988.

Began his career in finance and founded an investment banking firm in 1994. He says he and a partner bought a small musical instrument company in 1993 and grew it into Steinway Musical Instruments, which went public in 1996; he was its chairman for 17 years.
Serves as board chair of the Fresno Chaffee Zoo Corporation. He also founded the Kirkland Foundation, an animal rescue organization.
Ran in the 20th District in 2024 to succeed Kevin McCarthy, receiving 4.9 percent in the March special primary and 4.1 percent in the regular March 5 primary, and did not advance.
Launched his 2026 campaign against Costa on November 19, 2025, and finished second in the June 2, 2026 primary with 26.3 percent of the vote to Costa's 42.2 percent.

priorities.text: In his 2024 Ballotpedia survey, named the economy as central to his campaign, saying a 'healthy market economy with limited regulation is the key to reducing the high cost of living.'
Called for securing the border and returning to enforcement of immigration law, and for addressing property crime.

positions.summary: Supports securing the border and enforcing immigration law, saying the country should not tolerate 'free-for-all' border policies.
positions.quote: We need to secure our borders and return to the enforcement of immigration law.

positions.summary: Says Americans already pay enough in taxes and that government should focus on how tax dollars are spent rather than raising them.

researchNotes: Neither candidate has completed Ballotpedia's 2026 Candidate Connection survey; Kirkland's positions are drawn from his 2024 survey answers (for the adjoining 20th District race he ran in that year), which may not reflect any 2026 platform changes. Jim Costa's positions and priorities are drawn from his official House issues pages (costa.house.gov/issues), checked 2026-09-25. Federal key votes and FEC totals for the incumbent are added separately by script. Biographies were expanded in October 2026; Kyle Kirkland's own 2024 Ballotpedia survey is the main source for his early life, and sources differ slightly on his Steinway tenure (Ballotpedia says 1993-2011, his survey and the San Joaquin Valley Sun say 17 years), so only the 17-year figure is used.
